meta.note: Bilimsel sabitler resmi NASA/ESA kaynaklarından; 'gameplay' bloğu oyun dengesi ayarlarıdır.

marsGravity.note: Mean surface gravity on the NASA Mars Fact Sheet (3.71 in older documents is out of date).

lifeSupport.note: o2KgPerSol: BVAD Rev 2 Table 3-31, 0.895 kg per crew member per Earth day x 24.66/24 h. waterLPerSol: BVAD drinking water 2.00 kg per day.
lifeSupport.simplifiedNote: suitO2CapacityKg is a game value; the Advanced EMU stores about 0.77 kg (1.7 lbm) of usable O2 (ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20170009505).

eva.simplifiedNote: Real: NASA's Artemis xEVA suit supports EVAs of up to 8 h (6 ± 2 h) plus 1 h of backup O2, and traverses are planned at about 2 km/h (33 m/min) (xEVA System ConOps EVA-EXP-0042 Rev B). suitO2PctPerMin = 100 % / 480 min, so a full suit lasts the 8 h EVA; use is constant here (real use depends on workload) and the 1 h backup is not modelled. BVAD gives 0.086 kg O2 per EVA hour. Game values: speedMPerMin 45 m/min (faster than the 2 km/h planning pace); suit battery drain base 0.04 %/min + heater 0.21 %/min per 100 °C below 0 °C, chosen so a full battery heats the suit for the 8 h EVA at −80 °C (no Mars-suit heater power is published); suitCoolingFracPerMin 0.004 (time constant ≈ 250 min) so that with an empty battery at −80 °C the joints freeze after about 55 min and the suit reaches −15 °C after about 1.9 h; warming rates, the low-integrity penalty and all thresholds.

gameplay.simplifiedNote: Game balance block. Time is compressed: a sol is 24.66 h (constants.sol, NASA Mars Fact Sheet); at gameMinutesPerRealSecond 2 it lasts about 12.3 real minutes (12 h of daylight ≈ 6 min) and in the jury quick mode (?demo, demoGameMinutesPerRealSecond 4) about 6.2 min. The on-screen walking speed is not a separate value: it is eva.speedMPerMin × game minutes per real second ÷ metersPerPixel, so metres walked per game minute always equal eva.speedMPerMin.

deploy.note: Base systems land packed in cargo crates and are set up by the player on EVA (ux-plan #8). Minutes are game values; the minigame stands for the work (pointing the array, wiring MOXIE and the MAV, starting the greenhouse). Until the array is deployed the base runs on its battery (and RTG if chosen).

cargoBonus.note: K4 Sedef (nursedef design advisor): free payload mass carries extra consumables. Game values; 4 kg O2 + 10 L water is 14 kg, well inside a 15% margin of any rocket's Mars payload in this game.

launchWindow.simplifiedNote: Game values: crew morale at landing when the launch window is caught (90) or missed (80). Real: Earth-Mars launch windows open about every 26 months (constants.synodicPeriod, NASA Trajectory Browser); a missed window means a long wait on the ground, modelled here as extra cost and lower starting morale.

instrumentData.simplifiedNote: Game rule: each instrument dataMbit (instruments list) is its routine science and housekeeping volume per sol. It is downlinked automatically before the player report packets on every relay pass, so data-heavy instruments leave less room for reports. The per-instrument volumes are game values scaled to the game relay pass capacities (habitat.relayPasses), not measured instrument data volumes.

transit.simplifiedNote: Transit task chain (Earth -> Mars cruise). Real: the Mars 2020 cruise stage was solar-powered, and the spacecraft flew trajectory correction manoeuvres (TCMs) during cruise and approach (JPL Mars 2020 launch press kit). Everything below is a game value: okScore is the minigame quality needed for a nominal result; a degraded task costs, at landing, battery charge (okChargeFrac 0.9 vs degradedChargeFrac 0.6 of capacity), habitat O2 lost to the micrometeoroid leak (leakO2LossKg 3 ≈ 3 sols of habitat use at constants.lifeSupport.o2KgPerSol 0.92), MAV fuel spent on extra correction burns (tcmMavFuelLossPct 8; in reality TCM propellant comes from the cruise stage's own tanks, not from the ascent vehicle) and morale after a cold cruise (thermalMoraleLoss 10). scorePerTask and the time limits are game values; day and dose advance in equal chunks per task up to the orbit's transitDays.

rockets.name: Falcon Heavy
rockets.simplifiedNote: Game values scaled to the game's lander. Real: up to 16,800 kg to Mars (NASA LSP); NASA's Europa Clipper launch contract was about $178 M.

rockets.name: Vulcan Centaur
rockets.simplifiedNote: Game values scaled to the game's lander; a Mars payload figure for Vulcan Centaur was not found on an official page.

rockets.name: SLS Block 1B
rockets.simplifiedNote: Game values scaled to the game's lander. Real: Block 1B carries more than 27 t to TLI and Block 2 cargo more than 80,000 lb (36 t) to Mars (SLS Reference Guide); NASA OIG IG-22-003 puts one SLS at $2.2 B.

base.simplifiedNote: Habitat mass, cost and power loads are game values for a one-astronaut base. NASA DRA 5.0 Addendum estimates 12 kWe day and night for a crew-of-four habitat (www.nasa.gov/pdf/373667main_NASA-SP-2009-566-ADD.pdf).

terrain.simplifiedNote: Route layout, sand pit positions, the slowdown factor, ice dig values and the drone rule (Ingenuity scouts the route around sand pits) are game values. Wrecks are not shown until the player uncovers them by digging (explore.dig). Real lesson behind the sand pits: Spirit was stuck in soft sand at Troy (NASA Spirit mission page).

map.simplifiedNote: Compressed, fictional map (D-012, widened in the 2026-11-15 merge): base at 0 m; west, the glacier route to the ice wall (-5000 m, map edge -5350 m, terrain.westRegion); east, the lava-plain route through a dried lake bed, dunes and a crater field to a rubble-sealed lava-tube skylight (+1400 m). Distances are game values chosen for walking time and suit O2, not a real site survey. Inside the base area (-120 m .. 0 m) structures are drawn at sprite scale: -120 m maps to baseLeftPx.

westRegion.note: Phoenix found water ice just under the surface and saw frost form on the ground: the basis for an icy area.
westRegion.simplifiedNote: The western ice field, its lost cargo lander, the ice wall and every distance here are FICTIONAL game values on a compressed map, to be labelled as fiction in the game and on the project page. Distances are metres west of the airlock. The ice blocks across the glacier path, the hits needed to dig through them and the game minutes per hit are game values too. The trail signs follow what was really seen: Spirit dragged its broken right-front wheel from 2006 and left a furrow; HiRISE imaged Phoenix's parachute, backshell and heat-shield mark; Beagle 2 landed on airbags.

iceCave.note: Thick ice lies under a thin cover of rock and dust and is exposed where slopes erode.
iceCave.simplifiedNote: FICTIONAL: a walk-in cave in an ice bank has not been observed on Mars; it stands in for the buried ice exposed at scarps. The lost lander sealed inside it, the 6 hits needed to break the ice and 3 game minutes per hit are game values.

shelterCave.note: Thick, fairly pure water ice lies under a thin cover of rock and dust and is exposed where slopes erode: the ice the player chips into the bottle.
shelterCave.simplifiedNote: FICTIONAL (D-014, proposed): a walk-in ice cave on Mars has not been observed. It sits on the ice field before the glacier and the blizzard; inside it the ice field's extra cold and deep-cold heat loss do not reach the suit, and crises wait. Its position, the 2 L bottle, 15 game minutes to fill it and walking at 80% speed while carrying it are game values.

polygons.note: Phoenix landed among ice-rich polygons: patterned ground made by ice expanding and contracting.

glacier.note: Ice capped by a layer of ice-cemented rock and dust, exposed as blue ice at a steep scarp at its edge.

blizzard.note: Phoenix's lidar saw snow falling from clouds about 4 km above its site; the snow evaporated before reaching the ground.
blizzard.simplifiedNote: FICTIONAL: a ground blizzard that slows a walker has not been observed on Mars, and the thin air could not push a person this hard. Walking west into it drops to 45% speed, east with it to 85%, both at full strength from 3500 m. Game values, to be labelled as fiction.

finalProbe.note: Deep Space 2 (Amundsen and Scott): two microprobes carried by Mars Polar Lander in 1999, built to bury their forebody about 1 m into the south polar ground and look for water ice, while the aftbody stayed on the surface to relay data. All three were lost on arrival.
finalProbe.simplifiedNote: FICTIONAL placement: the probes were never found; putting one here, its 5 hits to dig out and its glint are game choices.

cold.simplifiedNote: FICTIONAL game values. The ice field is up to 35 C colder than the landing site, and from 1900 m the cold pulls heat out of the suit faster than its heaters can replace (up to 1.2 C per game minute at the ice wall). Phoenix, at a high northern latitude, measured the colder conditions that inspire this, but these numbers are not its measurements.

ufo.note: Viking 1 Cydonia 'Face on Mars' (1976) pareidolia olayına saygı duruşu olan kurgusal sahne.
